To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have designed a new class of micromachines, called magnetic helical micro swimmers (MHMS), and we have demonstrated their controlled in vivo swimming in a deep tissue.
we have designed and developed a new class of microrobotic helical swimmers that can swim autonomously in vivo, and that we have demonstrated that they can swim autonomously inside the body in vivo.

we have demonstrated in vivo imaging of a swarm of helical flagella and actuation of the same in a live mouse brain using external magnetic fields (magnetic tweezers) for the first time, which is a major milestone in this field.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and synthesis of novel functionalized nanomaterials and their integration with biological systems for the development of novel biomedical devices.
the design, fabrication, and characterization of a novel type of magnetic helical flagella, which is capable of controlled in vivo swimming in deep tissue.
the development of a new class of microrobots that can be used to manipulate and deliver drugs, cells, and other biological materials in the human body.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this work represents a major milestone in microrobotics.
we are now able to control the in vivo swimming of bacteria like micromotors.
the authors have demonstrated in vivo imaging and actuating a swarm of magnetic flagella like microrobots by external magnetic fields in deep tissue.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we demonstrated the first in vivo swimming of magnetic helical microrobots in deep tissue, and the first controlled in vivo swimming of bacterial-like magnetic microrobots.
it is the first demonstration that magnetic helical micro swimmers can be controlled in deep tissue.
we developed a new class of biocompatible micromachines, which can be used as a new generation of transporters in the field of synthetic biology and medicine.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a swarm of magnetic bacteria can be controlled remotely and precisely, in vivo, by external magnetic fields, which opens the door to the development of a new generation of microrobotic transporters with a wide range of biomedical applications, including assisted fertilization and drug/gene-delivery.
a swarm of helical microswimmer can be remotely controlled in vivo in deep tissue by an external magnetic field.
a swarm of bacteria-like flagella can be controlled in vivo.
